summary: Specifies the format of the DCLASS object used with RSVP and briefly discusses its use.

eli5.summary: This defines one small field in RSVP messages that carries a traffic priority label.

questions: what is the rsvp dclass object
what does dclass carry in rsvp
how does rsvp use diffserv code points
subtitle: A small RSVP object that carries DiffServ code points so an upstream sender or router knows how to mark packets.

tldr.problem: When RSVP requests cross a differentiated services (DS) network, the packets may need to be marked with a particular DSCP before they reach the network's ingress, and RSVP had no way to carry that value.
tldr.mechanism: The DCLASS object (Class Num 225) holds one or more DSCPs, one per 32-bit word, and a DS-network element adds it to the RESV message sent back upstream.
tldr.outcome: Senders or upstream egress routers can mark packets correctly. Modifying the object in flight could change the QoS a flow receives, so the RFC discusses the resulting attacks.

facts.label: DSCP position
facts.value: Six high-order bits of the least significant byte

today: RFC 2996 is a Proposed Standard (November 2000), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The surrounding framework is described in RFC 2998.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs to Carry DSCPs
sections.content:
RSVP signaling (RFC 2205) can request Quality of Service (QoS) and help manage it for application traffic in a differentiated service (diff-serv or DS) network. It is useful to carry Differentiated Services Code Points (DSCPs) in RSVP messages, for example to arrange marking of packets upstream of the DS network's ingress point, at the sender or at a previous network's egress router.

The document assumes standard RSVP senders and receivers, a diff-serv network somewhere between them, and at least one RSVP-aware network element in that network. That element may be a policy enforcement point (PEP) or may simply act as an admission control agent. It is typically a router.
sections.eli5: Some roads have fast lanes. This note tells traffic which lane sticker to wear before it reaches the road.

sections.title: How the Object Is Used
sections.content:
The sender composes a normal RSVP PATH message and sends it toward the receiver. It passes the PEPs or admission control agents of the DS network, which install state and forward it. If admission downstream succeeds, a RESV message comes back, and each RSVP-enabled element decides whether the flow is admissible to the diff-serv network.

If it is admissible, the appropriate service level (behavior aggregate) is determined. The element then either marks arriving packets itself using MF classification or asks for upstream marking. Upstream marking could happen anywhere before the ingress, most likely at the originating sender or at the egress boundary router of an upstream network. Where marking occurs can be settled by agreement or a negotiation protocol, which is outside the scope of the document.

For upstream marking, the element adds a DCLASS object with one or more DSCPs to the RESV message sent toward the sender. If the request is not admissible, it sends a RESV error message toward the receiver, and no DCLASS is required.

The object is meant as a general tool. The RFC's second example has the egress router choose the behavior aggregate while the ingress must do the marking, so DCLASS carries the marking information between them.
sections.eli5: The router at the gate decides which sticker the parcels need and writes it on a note that travels back to the sender.

sections.title: The DCLASS Object Format
sections.content:
The first 32-bit word is the standard RSVP object header, with Class Num 225. The length field gives the total object length in bytes, and the minimum is 8. After the header come one or more 32-bit words, each holding a DSCP in the six high-order bits of the least significant byte.

The number of DSCPs is (Length - 4) / 4. The network may return several DSCPs so the host can tell sub-flows within a behavior aggregate apart. For the AF PHB group (RFC 2597), the example is 001010, 001100 and 001110, for increasing drop precedence within Class 1. The document says nothing about the significance of their order.

The Class Num is taken from the space of unknown class objects that should be ignored and forwarded by nodes that do not recognize them, for maximal backward compatibility.
sections.eli5: The note has a short header and then a list of stickers, one per line, and routers that do not understand the note simply pass it along.

sections.title: Admission Control
sections.content:
From a black-box view, admission control and policy amount to deciding whether to accept a request and which DSCPs to use for its traffic. The details are out of scope. The decision rests on resource availability and on policy for using the diff-serv network's resources.

For resources, one or more elements in or at the edge of the DS network must understand the effect of admitting the flow and the availability of resources along the data path. For policy, the element may use identity objects describing users or applications in the request, and may act as a PEP/PDP using a policy database or directory.
sections.eli5: Before handing out a sticker, the gatekeeper checks that there is room on the fast lane and that you are allowed to use it.

sections.title: Simple Admission Control Tables
sections.content:
Appendix A recommends basic functionality for simple resource-based admission control in configurable standalone routers, assuming a single DSCP in the object. Two configurable tables are needed.

The first maps an intserv service type to a DSCP, in rows of the form Intserv service type : DSCP. It would typically hold at least Guaranteed, Controlled Load and Best-Effort service. Best-effort will typically map to DSCP 000000, but may be overridden. The second table has rows of the form DSCP : Token bucket profile, giving the total resources available in the diff-serv network for traffic in that DSCP's service class, to be used when admitting quantitative requests.
sections.eli5: Two cheat sheets: one says which sticker fits each kind of service, and one says how much room each sticker's lane has.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Changing the object could let a flow get more or less QoS than it should. A third party between the DS ingress node and the upstream marker could lower QoS to an unacceptable level without cutting off the flow completely, a subtle denial of service attack that is hard to detect.

Raising QoS by changing DCLASS is called less significant, since protection against hosts guessing good DSCPs and marking packets must already exist. If that protection and the marking were both pushed upstream, correct transmission of the object must be ensured to prevent theft of service.

Merely observing the object can also leak information: that flows receive different QoS, that a flow was promoted or demoted, and details about the DS network's internal operations.
sections.eli5: If someone swaps the sticker on the way, your parcels could be slowed down without anyone noticing, and anyone who reads the notes learns who gets the fast lane.
